title: Inventory and Postcards
premise: Astrid Whitlock has spent ten years cataloging the unfinished life of their best friend, Junie Vale, who vanished after a fire that killed two people — a fire Astrid believes Junie set to survive. When a late-night radio station plays a song Junie only ever sang once, in private, never recorded, Astrid realizes Junie is alive, nearby, and running out of time. Tracking her through the city's insomniac margins, Astrid must decide whether justice means turning her in or bearing witness to what survival cost her. The book ends with Astrid choosing neither law nor silence: they help Junie record the song, say the goodbye they owed for a decade, and let her go to face the consequences on her own terms — keeping only the postcards she sends from prison, which Astrid shelves, finally cataloged, in the library's public collection.
about_author: August Amberdale is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent six years cataloging unclaimed property for a municipal records office. Their fiction is drawn to the quiet crimes of ordinary survival and the people who keep other people's secrets alive.

chapters.title: The Hours Between Two and Four
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. We meet the night library, its insomniac regulars, and Astrid's ritual of shelving a box of Junie's unsent postcards that no one else knows exists. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as routine, and the ache of a decade-old unfinished sentence.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Driving home at dawn, a radio DJ plays an unnamed song Astrid recognizes instantly — Junie's, sung once in a stairwell ten years ago, never written down. Astrid calls the station; the caller before them requested it anonymously. Emotional beat: the dead coming back to life in three minutes of static.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took, What It Left
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Astrid's POV. The night of the Harlan Street fire: two deaths, Junie's disappearance, Astrid's lie to the police about where Junie was. Emotional beat: the origin of the guilt — Astrid didn't just lose Junie, they helped her vanish.

chapters.title: The Caller Before Me
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid tracks the DJ, Marisol, who remembers the caller: a woman with a coastal accent who said 'play this for the one who kept my things.' Astrid realizes Junie knows exactly where they are — and is reaching out. Emotional beat: hope arriving as a dare.

chapters.title: Postcard, Undated
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Among Junie's postcards Astrid finds one that was never blank: a single line, 'Don't look for me until the song finds you.' It's been there for years, waiting to mean something. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing you've been part of a plan you never agreed to.

chapters.title: The City That Sleeps Less
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid begins haunting the all-night places — laundromats, ferry terminals, a 24-hour diner — following the song's lyrics like a map, each verse naming a location from their shared past. Emotional beat: grief turning investigative, the past becoming terrain.

chapters.title: Detective Okafor, Ten Years Later
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. The detective who never closed the Harlan Street case has kept a file he shouldn't have, including a photo of Astrid outside the burned building. He visits the library, ostensibly to donate books. Emotional beat: the law as a patient, courteous predator.

chapters.title: Verse Two: The Laundromat
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At the laundromat from the song's second verse, a woman matches Junie's description — but it's her sister Dee, who reveals Junie has been in touch, that she's sick, and that she's been 'putting her affairs in order' for months. Emotional beat: the clock starting to tick audibly.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival, Itemized
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Dee recounts what Junie confessed: the fire was arson, an escape from the man who owned the building and owned Junie's debts, and the two who died were collateral Junie has never forgiven herself for. Emotional beat: sympathy and horror holding hands — survival was never free.

chapters.title: What Astrid Almost Said
chapters.summary: Flashback, Astrid's POV. The stairwell, the song, and the confession Astrid swallowed — that they loved Junie, and that they would have burned it all down with her. Emotional beat: the decade of 'almost' given its true shape.

chapters.title: Okafor's File
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor lays out his evidence: the song on the radio is the first new thread in ten years, and he's been listening too. He confronts Astrid gently, offering a deal — help him find her, and Astrid's obstruction charge disappears. Emotional beat: temptation wearing the face of mercy.

chapters.title: Verse Four: The Ferry Terminal
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid follows the song to the terminal and finds a locker key taped under a bench, inside it a fresh postcard: 'You always were slow at finding things. One verse left. Come say it properly.' Emotional beat: terror and joy in the same breath — she's alive, she's near, she's asking.

chapters.title: Marisol's Late Shift
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The DJ reveals the anonymous caller visits the station every few weeks, always requesting the same unreleased song from a burned CD left in her mailbox. She gives Astrid the next drop date — three days away — and admits she's been sitting on the story for a year. Emotional beat: a stranger choosing complicity out of respect for a good song.

chapters.title: The Confession Astrid Keeps for Someone Else
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid tells Okafor a partial truth — that Junie is alive, that she's dying, that she wants to surrender but on her own terms — and asks for forty-eight hours. Okafor, against every rule, gives him thirty-six. Emotional beat: two keepers of the same secret negotiating its price.

chapters.title: Verse Five: The Lighthouse Road
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The final verse leads to the abandoned coastguard station where they were seventeen and invincible. Junie is there, thinner, oxygen tank in a duffel, unembarrassed and exactly herself. Emotional beat: the collapse of ten years of longing into an ordinary, devastating 'hello.'

chapters.title: Ten Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Alternating Astrid and Junie POV. Through one long night they trade the truths they withheld: the arson, the deaths, Astrid's lie, the love neither named. Junie asks Astrid to help her record the song properly before she turns herself in. Emotional beat: the 'almost' finally said, out loud, and it not being enough — and being enough.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. With Marisol's portable equipment, they record the song at dawn in the coastguard station, Junie's voice fraying on the last verse. She dictates a final postcard to be mailed after her surrender. Emotional beat: making something permanent out of a person who is running out of time.

chapters.title: Okafor at the Door
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor arrives at the station — he followed Astrid, of course he did — and finds Junie waiting with her written confession, her lawyer's number, and no intention of running. He reads the confession in silence. Emotional beat: the law meeting a justice it can't improve on, and a man deciding what his badge is for.

chapters.title: The Goodbye, Properly
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At the courthouse steps, Astrid says the goodbye they've owed for ten years — not 'goodbye' but everything underneath it. Junie goes through the doors without looking back, because looking back was the old way. Emotional beat: grief finally finished instead of merely endured.

chapters.title: Sentencing
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. The trial compresses into a single day; Okafor testifies to her cooperation and her sickness, and the sentence lands at seven years — mercy with a price tag. Dee and Astrid sit together in the gallery, strangers who share a person. Emotional beat: justice outside the law having cleared the way for justice inside it.

chapters.title: Postcards, Cataloged
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Months later, the prison postcards arrive on schedule, and Astrid does the thing they've avoided: shelves them in the library's public collection under 'Vale, J. — correspondence, complete.' Patrons start reading them. Emotional beat: turning a private grief into a public gift.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, closing. On the radio, the recorded song plays in full, credited to Junie Vale, and the night library fills with people who came to listen. Astrid takes inventory of what survival cost and what it left — Dee, Marisol, Okafor, the song, the shelf — and, for the first time, finds the count acceptable. Emotional beat: found family assembled from the wreckage, and the long 'almost' at last at rest.
